definition: Daunting means intimidating — so difficult or overwhelming in prospect that it makes you doubt your courage before you even begin.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word daunting. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know daunting should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: On her first morning at the new job, the training binder alone looked daunting — three hundred pages to master before Friday.
A challenging task stretches your skills but still feels doable; a daunting one makes you hesitate before you even start.
Overwhelming goes further than daunting — the task no longer just intimidates you, it feels bigger than anything you could possibly handle.

Intimidating means making you feel nervous or outmatched, and anything can do it — a fierce boss, a marble lobby, a test. Daunting is narrower: it describes the task or prospect itself, whose sheer size or difficulty drains your courage before you begin. People are intimidating; the climb ahead is daunting.

Formidable describes something whose size, power, or skill inspires fear and respect — a formidable opponent, a formidable intellect. The word admires the thing itself. Daunting keeps the focus on you: a daunting task is one that shakes your nerve at the prospect, whatever anyone else thinks of it.

Discouraging things drain your hope along the way — poor results, slow progress, a string of rejections. Daunting works earlier: a daunting task intimidates you before you have started, when nothing has gone wrong yet. Discouragement comes from setbacks; daunting is how the starting line itself can look.

It pairs most naturally with words like task, challenge, and prospect: 'a daunting challenge,' 'a daunting prospect.'

When Priya agreed to digitize the historical society's photo collection, she pictured a weekend of pleasant sorting.
Then the volunteers led her to the storage room.
Boxes rose from floor to ceiling along every wall — eleven thousand photographs, most of them unlabeled, some fused together by decades of humidity.
The society's only scanner was older than she was, and the catalog existed mainly in the memory of a ninety-year-old former librarian.
Standing in the doorway with her clipboard, Priya felt the daunting size of what she had promised before she had scanned a single frame.
So she did the only thing that makes such a job shrink: she labeled one box, then the next, letting the wall of boxes become a line of small, finishable tasks.
